sophie: Heads-up — saw a weird pattern in perf traces today where tenants with lots of long-history context get effectively deprioritized during sustained load. Not classic "starvation" but their requests show large queue wait spikes and tiny batch slots. :thinking:

arjun: saw that earlier in profiling. KV hit rate is fine but batch formation favors short sequences and they get stitched into high-turnover mini-batches. Long ones keep being preempted.

mike: can you paste the flame/profile?

sophie: pasted snippet from the trace (trimmed):
```
batcher: avg_wait_short=12ms avg_wait_long=240ms
kv_lookup: avg=3.8ms overall_hit=82%
alloc_slice: short_batches=72% token_target=64k long_batches=8% token_target=256k
queue_reorders=1.4k/hour
```

arjun: thanks. Looks like the batching heuristic's `slice_threshold` and `age_preference` are tuned for latency-first workloads which creates a sawtooth where long sequences get late/rare slots. Our kernel selection logic also prefers small-mini-batches for memory locality which compounds this.

sophie: proposal: try a "preemptive slice allocation" where we reserve a small fraction of the token budget per cycle for long-running contexts and tenants with high-avg-seqlen. Not full priority, just earmark to avoid long tails.

jen: +1 on earmarking. We should be careful with unit economics — reserved tokens still consume GPU cycles. Maybe make it adaptive: start with 5% of tokens -> measure fairness delta -> ramp to 15% if tail persists.

mike: can we implement without touching kernel selector? My concern is changing batch formation semantics might degrade latency for short calls.

arjun: we can add it as a queue policy layer only. Rough config prototype: 
```yaml
queue_policy:
  name: preemptive_slice_v1
  token_budget_cycle_ms: 50
  reserve_fraction_for_long: 0.05
  long_seq_threshold_tokens: 128
  tenant_earmark_mode: dynamic  # static | dynamic
  dynamic_scale:
    metric: tail_wait_95
    up_threshold_ms: 200
    down_threshold_ms: 80
```

sophie: test plan idea: rollout on a single cell, pick 10 tenants (mix of long/short profiles), run synthetic replay + production shadow for 2 hours. Metrics to watch: p95_wait by seq_len, batch_util, tokens/sec, and per-tenant throughput.

jen: also add regression gates: no more than 3% increase in short-request p50 latency and no more than 1.5% drop in overall tokens/sec. If breached -> auto-disable.

mike: i ran a micro-sim this morning. With reserve_fraction=0.05 long p95 drops ~35% and short p50 up ~1.1%. So looks promising. I can push a canary config to staging.

arjun: good. One more thing: KV cache behavior — long contexts often have large KV footprints and cause frequent cache evictions. If we reserve slices but don't adjust KV budget awareness, we might thrash kernels. Suggest adding a small KV pressure signal to the decision rule so we avoid scheduling many long sequences when cache miss rate > 20%.

sophie: agreed. Add a circuit: if kv_miss_rate > 0.2 then scale down reserve_fraction by 50% until tollerable.

jen: we should codify the experiments and ownership:
- impl: mike (batcher) + arjun (scheduler)
- metric dashboards: sophie
- rollback hook: ops-bot will auto-disable on gate breach

ops-bot: Note: canary deployment scheduled to cell r3-phi at 2025-11-18T09:40:00Z. Automated checks: token-rate, p50/p95 per-class, kv_miss.

mike: will open PR with the config and a short simulator script. I'll include a seed that reproduces the sawtooth.

arjun: once we have sim and canary results, next step is kernel selector tweak: prefer kernels that are more throughput-friendly for mixed-size mini-batches — but only if canary shows reserve helps fairness.

sophie: thanks all. If canary looks good, we can try gradual ramp across two more cells and then consider tenant-level policies (opt-in fair-share) for high-cost customers. :thumbsup:

jen: nice work. Please paste the PR/links here when ready.

mike: PR up in ~2 hrs. 

sophie: cool, i'll start the dashboard tiles and baseline captures now.

arjun: tagging ops for visibility: @ops on standby?

ops-bot: @ops notified.
